books.title: It's Not Luck
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
key_concepts: Sequel to The Goal: Alex Rogo runs a group of companies
Constraint moves from plant to market
Thinking Processes: CRT, Evaporating Cloud, FRT, PRT, TT
Find the core conflict below many undesirable effects (UDEs)
Segment the market; do not cut price for all
Policy constraints are more common than physical constraints
books.link_to_goal: Applies The Goal's three questions with formal Thinking Process trees, after the constraint moves from production to the market.

tools.why: Evaporating Cloud (conflict diagram): Objective A <- need B <- want D; A <- need C <- want D'; D conflicts with D'. Write the assumption under each arrow; break one assumption with an injection.

Current Reality Tree: List 5-10 UDEs; connect with if-then sufficiency logic; the entity that causes about 70% of UDEs is the core problem. | Future Reality Tree with negative branch reservations: Injection -> if-then chain -> desired effects; test each step for new UDEs.

books.title: Critical Chain
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
key_concepts: TOC applied to projects
Critical chain = longest chain of dependent tasks including resource contention
Task estimates hold hidden safety; Student Syndrome and Parkinson's Law waste it
Remove safety from tasks; pool it in a project buffer
Feeding buffers protect the critical chain from non-critical paths
Multitasking stretches all lead times
Buffer management: track buffer consumed vs chain complete
Relay-runner work rule
books.link_to_goal: Moves The Goal from plant to projects: the critical chain is Herbie, pooled buffers replace local safety, and multitasking is the new excess WIP.

tools.why: Buffer fever chart: Plot % project buffer consumed vs % critical chain complete. Zones: green (consumed < complete), yellow, red (act).

Aggressive estimate + pooled project buffer: Cut each task estimate to ~50% confidence; project buffer ~= 50% of the cut sum (or root-sum-square of cuts). | Stop bad multitasking: Limit active projects (staggering on the constraint resource); finish one task before you start the next.

books.title: The Haystack Syndrome
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
key_concepts: Data is not information; information answers a question
Throughput accounting: T, I, OE replace cost accounting for decisions
Product cost allocation gives wrong decisions
Rank products by throughput per constraint unit
Information system design: schedule the constraint first (DBR)
Buffer origins: find causes of buffer holes
books.link_to_goal: Turns The Goal's T, I, OE measures into throughput accounting and a constraint-first scheduling information system.

tools.why: Throughput per constraint unit (T/CU): T = price - truly variable cost; rank items by T / (minutes on constraint). Fill constraint from the top.
Throughput accounting decision test: Accept a change if delta NP = delta T - delta OE > 0; ROI = (T - OE) / I.
Buffer hole analysis: Record which resource caused each late arrival into the buffer; Pareto the causes.

books.title: Necessary But Not Sufficient
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt, Eli Schragenheim, Carol A. Ptak
key_concepts: Business novel about an ERP software company
Technology is necessary but not sufficient for benefit
A technology gives benefit only if it removes a limitation
You must also change the rules that existed because of that limitation
Six questions to evaluate any technology
Goldratt's six questions for technology
Rule change check
books.link_to_goal: Applies The Goal's constraint logic to software: a tool helps only if it removes a limitation and the old rules change too.

books.title: Isn't It Obvious?
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt, Ilan Eshkoli, Joe Brownleer
key_concepts: Business novel about a retail chain
Forecast error is lower at aggregate (central warehouse) than at the store
Hold stock at the central point; replenish stores often in small amounts
Replenish to actual consumption (pull), not to forecast
Dynamic Buffer Management: adjust target levels by buffer color
Fewer stockouts and less excess inventory at the same time
Aggregation of variation
books.link_to_goal: Applies The Goal's buffers and pull to retail distribution: aggregate stock and replenish to consumption.

tools.why: Replenish to consumption: Each period, order quantity = units consumed since last order; target = max expected demand over reliable replenishment time. | Dynamic Buffer Management (DBM): Split target into thirds. Too long in red -> raise target ~33%; too long in green -> cut ~33%.

books.title: The Choice
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt, Efrat Goldratt-Ashlag
key_concepts: Dialogue between Goldratt and his daughter
Inherent simplicity: more connections in a system means fewer points that control it
Every conflict can be removed; do not accept compromise
People are good: look for the logic, not blame
Never say 'I know'; keep testing
Clear thinking is a learnable skill
Inherent simplicity search
Assume people are good
books.link_to_goal: Explains the philosophy behind The Goal: inherent simplicity means few points (constraints) control a complex system.

books.title: The Race
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt, Robert E. Fox
key_concepts: Inventory is a competitive weapon (lead time, quality, engineering)
Drum-buffer-rope scheduling explained with figures
Troop march analogy: slowest soldier, rope from front to slowest
Time buffers protect the constraint, not stock everywhere
Comparison with JIT/kanban and MRP
books.link_to_goal: Explains The Goal's DBR and the Herbie hike with figures, and argues low inventory is a competitive edge.

tools.why: Drum-buffer-rope: Drum = constraint schedule; buffer = time of work queued before drum; rope = release material at (drum time - buffer time). | Time buffer sizing: Start buffer ~ 1/2 to 1/3 of current lead time; adjust with buffer penetration data.

books.title: Theory of Constraints (What Is This Thing Called Theory of Constraints and How Should It Be Implemented?)
books.author: Eliyahu M. Goldratt
key_concepts: Five focusing steps defined formally
Throughput world vs cost world
Necessary condition and goal
Thinking Process introduced: Current Reality Tree, Evaporating Cloud
Effect-cause-effect reasoning
Measures must link local decisions to the goal
books.link_to_goal: Formal short statement of the five focusing steps and the thinking tools Alex uses informally in The Goal.

tools.why: Five focusing steps: 1 Identify the constraint. 2 Exploit it. 3 Subordinate all else. 4 Elevate it. 5 If it moves, go to 1; do not let inertia be the constraint.
Effect-cause-effect: Hypothesize a cause; predict another effect it must also cause; verify that effect.

books.title: Goldratt's Rules of Flow: The Principles of The Goal Applied to Projects
books.author: Efrat Goldratt-Ashlag
key_concepts: Business novel; applies The Goal's flow rules to projects
Rule: improve flow is the primary objective
Rule: limit work released (do not start too early)
Rule: local efficiency is not the target
Rule: focus on the few points that block flow
Full-kit: do not start a task until all inputs are ready
Remove multitasking; stagger project starts
Full-kit gate
books.link_to_goal: Restates The Goal's flow rules for projects: choke release, full-kit, stop multitasking, focus on the flow-blocking resource.

tools.why: Choke release: Release new projects only at the constraint's pace; freeze a share of open projects.
Flow priority rule: Priority by buffer consumption, not by who asks loudest.

books.title: The Logical Thinking Process: A Systems Approach to Complex Problem Solving
books.author: H. William Dettmer
key_concepts: Practitioner manual for TOC Thinking Process trees
Intermediate Objectives Map (goal tree) as first step
Categories of Legitimate Reservation: rules to check logic
Current Reality Tree, Evaporating Cloud, Future Reality Tree, Prerequisite Tree
Strategy and policy use, not only production
books.link_to_goal: Practical manual for the Thinking Process tools that answer The Goal's what-to-change questions.

tools.why: Intermediate Objectives Map (goal tree): Goal at top; 3-5 critical success factors; necessary conditions below; logic = 'in order to... we must...'. | Prerequisite Tree: Objective -> obstacles -> intermediate objectives that overcome each; order them.
Categories of Legitimate Reservation (CLR): Check clarity, entity existence, causality existence, cause sufficiency, additional cause, cause-effect reversal, predicted effect, tautology.

books.title: Goldratt's Theory of Constraints: A Systems Approach to Continuous Improvement
books.author: H. William Dettmer
key_concepts: Systems view of TOC
Five focusing steps and Thinking Processes as one system
Five original trees: CRT, EC, FRT, PRT, Transition Tree
Worked examples and exercises
Constraint as weakest link in a chain
books.link_to_goal: Systems explanation of TOC: The Goal's bottleneck as weakest link, plus the five Thinking Process trees.

tools.why: Transition Tree: Action + need -> expected effect, in step order, to reach an objective.
Chain analogy test: Ask: if I improve this link, does system output change? If no, it is not the constraint.

books.title: Velocity: Combining Lean, Six Sigma and the Theory of Constraints to Achieve Breakthrough Performance
books.author: Dee Jacob, Suzan Bergland, Jeff Cox
key_concepts: Business novel by co-author of The Goal
TOC finds where to focus; Lean removes waste; Six Sigma removes variation
Apply Lean and Six Sigma at the constraint first
Velocity = speed with direction toward the goal
Local Lean/Six Sigma projects off the constraint give no system gain
books.link_to_goal: Combines Lean and Six Sigma under The Goal's focusing: improve at the bottleneck first; other gains are mirages.

tools.why: Focus improvement at constraint: Rank improvement projects by delta T at constraint; skip work at non-constraints.
Variation reduction at constraint: Measure variation of the constraint input and cycle time; reduce it first.

books.title: Management Dilemmas: The Theory of Constraints Approach to Problem Identification and Solutions
books.author: Eli Schragenheim
key_concepts: Short case stories of managers in dilemmas
Reader solves first, then reads TOC analysis
Evaporating Cloud as everyday tool
Look past details to the core cause
Measures and policies cause most dilemmas
Case-first learning
books.link_to_goal: Case drills in Jonah-style reasoning: find the policy or measure that causes a management dilemma, as Alex does.

tools.why: Evaporating Cloud drill: For each dilemma, write the cloud and three assumptions per arrow before you decide.

books.title: Supply Chain Management at Warp Speed: Integrating the System from End to End
books.author: Eli Schragenheim, H. William Dettmer, J. Wayne Patterson
key_concepts: Simplified Drum-Buffer-Rope (S-DBR): market is the drum
Buffer management with green/yellow/red zones
Planned load on the constraint sets reliable due dates
Make-to-stock and make-to-order in one system
Distribution replenishment by consumption
books.link_to_goal: Simplifies The Goal's DBR into S-DBR with one time buffer and buffer-color priorities across the supply chain.

tools.why: Simplified DBR: Release order at (due date - production buffer). Priority = % buffer consumed.
Planned load check: Planned load = sum of constraint work for accepted orders / capacity; quote date = today + planned load + 1/2 buffer.
Buffer color priority: Green <33% consumed, yellow 33-67%, red >67%; work red first; >100% = late.

books.title: The Phoenix Project
books.author: Gene Kim, Kevin Behr, George Spafford
key_concepts: Business novel modeled on The Goal, set in IT operations
Four types of work: business projects, internal projects, changes, unplanned work
Brent: one expert is the constraint; all work queues on him
Three Ways: flow, feedback, continual learning
Unplanned work destroys planned work
Make work visible with a kanban board; freeze changes
Wait time = % busy / % idle
Three Ways
books.link_to_goal: Retells The Goal in IT: Brent is Herbie, Erik is Jonah, unplanned work and WIP replace plant inventory.

tools.why: Four types of work: Classify each item: business project, internal project, change, unplanned. Track the unplanned share. | Kanban board with WIP limits: Columns = steps; cards = work; limit cards per column.
Protect the constraint (Brent): Route all requests for the constraint through one queue; offload work others can do; document his know-how.
Wait-time rule of thumb: Wait ~ % busy / % idle (50% busy -> 1 unit; 90% -> 9 units; 99% -> 99).

books.title: The Unicorn Project
books.author: Gene Kim
key_concepts: Same story as Phoenix from a developer's view
Five Ideals: locality and simplicity; focus, flow and joy; improvement of daily work; psychological safety; customer focus
Core vs context work
Developer productivity depends on fast feedback and low coupling
Pay down technical debt as improvement of daily work
Five Ideals check
Core vs context split
books.link_to_goal: Shows The Goal's step 5: after Phoenix fixes ops, the constraint moves to dev coupling and feedback loops.

books.title: The Principles of Product Development Flow
books.author: Donald G. Reinertsen
key_concepts: Economic view: quantify cost of delay
Queues are the main hidden cost in product development
Variability is not always bad; manage its economic effect
Reduce batch size
WIP constraints; control queues not timelines
Fast feedback; decentralized control with economic rules
Cadence and synchronization
books.link_to_goal: Puts The Goal into economic terms for knowledge work: cost of delay, queue control, WIP limits and small batches.

tools.why: Cost of delay (CoD): CoD = value lost per unit time of delay (e.g. $/week). Quantify it for each item. | WSJF / CD3: Priority = CoD / duration (CD3). Do highest first.
WIP constraints: Cap WIP per stage or system; block start when at cap.
Queue size control: Monitor queues (not timelines); act when queue passes a limit.
Batch size reduction: Total cost = transaction cost (falls with batch size) + holding cost (rises); optimum is U-curve flat, so err small.
Kingman-based load rule: Queue time ~ rho/(1-rho); do not load near 100%.

books.title: Factory Physics
books.author: Wallace J. Hopp, Mark L. Spearman
key_concepts: Laws of manufacturing behavior from queueing theory
Little's Law: WIP = TH x CT
Kingman/VUT: wait = variability x utilization x process time
Critical WIP W0 = rb x T0
Best case, worst case, practical worst case performance
Variability buffering: inventory, capacity or time always pays for variability
CONWIP pull system
Variability buffering law
books.link_to_goal: Gives the queueing math behind The Goal: VUT explains fluctuations and idle non-bottlenecks; Little's Law and critical WIP size buffers.

tools.why: Kingman / VUT equation: CTq = ((ca^2 + ce^2)/2) x (u/(1-u)) x te
Little's Law: WIP = TH x CT
Critical WIP and best/worst/PWC: W0 = rb x T0; best CT = max(T0, w/rb); worst CT = w x T0; PWC CT = T0 + (w-1)/rb, PWC TH = w/(W0 + w - 1) x rb
CONWIP: Keep total WIP constant: start one only when one finishes.

books.title: Little's Law (chapter in Building Intuition: Insights from Basic Operations Management Models and Principles)
books.author: John D. C. Little, Stephen C. Graves
key_concepts: L = lambda x W for any stable system
Holds for averages over long time; no distribution assumptions
Finite-interval form holds with boundary error
Know two values, compute the third
Operations form: WIP = throughput x flow time
Use to check data consistency
books.link_to_goal: Proves The Goal's inventory claim: at fixed throughput, lead time falls in proportion to WIP.

tools.why: Little's Law: L = lambda W (WIP = TH x CT). Assumes conservation (arrivals ~= departures over the window). | Data consistency check: Compare measured avg WIP with TH x avg CT over the same window; large gap means bad data or unstable system.

books.title: Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production
books.author: Taiichi Ohno
key_concepts: Two pillars: just-in-time and jidoka (automation with a human touch)
Seven wastes; overproduction is the worst
Kanban as pull signal and information system
Ask why five times
Leveling production (heijunka)
Standard work
Small lots and fast setup
Five whys
Seven wastes
Jidoka / stop on defect
books.link_to_goal: Origin of pull and waste ideas that parallel The Goal: overproduction = activation without need; kanban is a distributed rope.

tools.why: Kanban pull signal: Make only when a downstream signal (card/slot) is free.

books.title: Lean Thinking
books.author: James P. Womack, Daniel T. Jones
key_concepts: Five principles: value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection
Value defined by the customer
Muda: activity that uses resources but gives no value
Flow: single-piece flow instead of batch and queue
Pull: make only what the customer asks for
Case studies of lean conversions
Five lean principles
books.link_to_goal: Generalizes Toyota ideas into five principles; flow and pull match The Goal's batch and release logic.

tools.why: Value-added ratio: VA ratio = value-added time / total lead time.

books.title: Learning to See: Value Stream Mapping to Add Value and Eliminate Muda
books.author: Mike Rother, John Shook
key_concepts: Value stream map (VSM): material and information flow on one page
Current state map, future state map, plan
Takt time sets the pace
Pacemaker process: one point schedules the stream
Supermarkets and FIFO lanes between processes
Timeline: lead time vs processing time
books.link_to_goal: Mapping method that shows where inventory and waiting sit; the pacemaker is The Goal's drum.

tools.why: Value stream map: Map steps, inventory triangles, information flow; timeline with lead time vs process time. | Takt time: Takt = available work time / customer demand.
FIFO lane with max: Fixed max queue between steps; upstream stops when full.

books.title: Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change for Your Technology Business
books.author: David J. Anderson
key_concepts: Visualize work
Limit WIP
Manage flow; measure lead time
Make policies explicit
Classes of service (expedite, fixed date, standard, intangible)
Start with what you do now; evolve
Began from TOC/DBR experiments at Microsoft and Corbis
Explicit policies
books.link_to_goal: Software kanban grew from DBR: WIP limits are the rope, classes of service set buffer priority.

tools.why: WIP limits per column: Do not pull a card into a column at its limit. | Classes of service: Assign each item a class by cost-of-delay shape; each class has a policy.

books.title: The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning Organization
books.author: Peter M. Senge
key_concepts: Five disciplines: personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, systems thinking
Reinforcing and balancing feedback loops; delays
System archetypes
Limits to Growth: growth loop meets a balancing limit
Shifting the Burden: symptomatic fix weakens fundamental fix
Beer Game: structure causes behavior
Small changes at leverage points
books.link_to_goal: Systems thinking for The Goal: Limits to Growth = constraint; Beer Game = matchstick game; Shifting the Burden = expediting habit.

tools.why: Limits to Growth archetype: Reinforcing growth loop + balancing loop from a limit; rule: do not push growth, remove the limit. | Shifting the Burden archetype: Symptom fix (fast) and fundamental fix (slow); side effect of symptom fix weakens the fundamental fix. | Causal loop diagram: Variables with +/- links; R and B loops; mark delays. | Fixes that Fail / Eroding Goals / Tragedy of the Commons: Other archetypes; check each against a recurring problem.

books.title: Out of the Crisis
books.author: W. Edwards Deming
key_concepts: Fourteen points for management
Common-cause vs special-cause variation
Most problems come from the system, not the worker
Tampering: reacting to common-cause noise makes it worse
Seven deadly diseases (e.g. focus on short-term profit, performance rating)
PDSA cycle (Shewhart cycle)
Red Bead experiment (later seminars)
PDSA cycle
No tampering rule
books.link_to_goal: Statistical base for The Goal's fluctuations: tell common from special cause; fix the system, not the worker.

tools.why: Control chart (XmR / process behavior chart): Center = mean; limits = mean +/- 2.66 x mean moving range. Point outside = special cause.

books.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer
books.author: Donella H. Meadows
key_concepts: Stocks and flows
Balancing and reinforcing feedback loops
Delays cause oscillation
Bounded rationality
System traps (policy resistance, drift to low performance, rule beating, seeking the wrong goal)
Twelve leverage points; goals and paradigms are strongest
Shifting dominance of loops
Leverage points list
System traps check
books.link_to_goal: Stock-flow language for The Goal: WIP is a stock, the constraint is the limiting factor, wrong measures are a system trap.

tools.why: Stock-and-flow model: Stock(t+1) = Stock(t) + inflow - outflow.

books.title: The DevOps Handbook
books.author: Gene Kim, Jez Humble, Patrick Debois, John Willis
key_concepts: Practice guide for the Three Ways
Deployment pipeline and continuous delivery
Small batches; trunk-based development
Telemetry; fast feedback
Value stream mapping for technology
Blameless post-mortems; learning culture
Find and elevate constraints in the delivery pipeline
Deployment pipeline
Blameless post-mortem
books.link_to_goal: Practice manual for The Goal ideas in software delivery: find the pipeline constraint, cut batch size, add fast feedback.

tools.why: Typical constraint progression: Environment creation -> code deployment -> test setup and run -> overly tight architecture -> product development.

books.title: Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps
books.author: Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, Gene Kim
key_concepts: Four key metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore
Speed and stability are not a trade-off
24 capabilities drive performance
Survey-based research (State of DevOps)
Westrum organizational culture
Lean management and WIP limits predict performance
Four key metrics (DORA)
Capability assessment
books.link_to_goal: Gives software a measured version of The Goal's global metrics: four key metrics replace local productivity measures.

books.title: Actionable Agile Metrics for Predictability
books.author: Daniel S. Vacanti
key_concepts: Flow metrics: WIP, cycle time, throughput, work item age
Little's Law assumptions and how to keep them
Cumulative flow diagram (CFD)
Cycle time scatterplot with percentile lines
Monte Carlo forecasting from throughput history
Service level expectation (SLE)
Pull policy: finish before start
books.link_to_goal: Measures The Goal's flow in knowledge work: CFD shows WIP and lead time, Monte Carlo replaces single-point plans.

tools.why: Cumulative flow diagram: Stacked count of items that have entered each state over time; vertical gap = WIP; horizontal gap = approx cycle time; top slope = arrival rate; bottom slope = throughput. | Cycle time scatterplot: Dot per finished item (date, cycle time); draw 50/85/95th percentile lines. | Work item age: Age = today - start; compare with SLE percentile.
Monte Carlo forecast: Sample daily throughput history N times to make a distribution of 'how many by date' or 'when for N items'; report 85th percentile.
Little's Law assumptions: Arrivals ~= departures; all started items finish; WIP age stable; consistent units.
